Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the NovaVolt Motors Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to NovaVolt Motors' Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, CEO; Marcus Hale, CFO; Dr. Liam Chen, Chief Manufacturing Officer; Sophia Grant, Chief Technology Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Elena Vasquez.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 2024 was a significant quarter for NovaVolt Motors, marked by progress across our key strategic initiatives. We achieved notable milestones in raw material sourcing and cost management, gross margin expansion per vehicle, delivery volume growth with clear guidance by model, factory expansions and operational efficiency improvements, managing the impact of raw material costs and supply chain disruptions, and updates on supply chain constraints with effective mitigation strategies. We are particularly pleased with the initial customer response to our Thunder full-size pickup, and its contribution to our backlog is substantial, now standing at over 450,000 units.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Marcus Hale to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Marcus Hale:
Thank you, Elena. Good morning, everyone. For Q3 2024, our revenue reached $2.8 billion, demonstrating a 65% increase compared to the same period last year. Our gross margin stood at 24.5%, reflecting our commitment to operational excellence. Operating expenses amounted to $650 million, and net income was $420 million. We maintain a robust financial position with $3.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Our outlook for the upcoming quarter is strong, guiding revenue to $3.2 billion to $3.5 billion, with continued margin expansion.

As we dive deeper into our financials, I'd like to highlight one of our key operational pillars: raw material sourcing and cost management. In the EV industry, where battery metals represent upwards of 40-50% of our cost of goods sold—or COGS—this is mission-critical for preserving EBITDA margins and scaling profitability. We've made significant strides here, navigating a volatile commodity landscape to deliver sequential cost reductions and enhanced supply chain resilience.

In Q3, our average battery pack cost per kilowatt-hour fell to $92 per kWh, down 8% quarter-over-quarter and 22% year-over-year. This puts us on track to hit our full-year target of under $90 per kWh by Q4, aligning with the industry's push toward the $60-70 per kWh threshold needed for true cost parity with internal combustion engine vehicles. Overall raw material costs as a percentage of revenue improved to 28% from 34% a year ago, contributing roughly 450 basis points to our gross margin expansion this quarter.

The past 18 months have been a rollercoaster for battery metals. Lithium carbonate equivalent—or LCE—prices, which peaked at over $80,000 per metric ton in late 2022 amid the post-IR-1 supply crunch, have corrected sharply to around $12,500 per metric ton today, an 85% drawdown. Nickel, critical for high-energy-density NMC cathodes, hovered at $16,000 per metric ton in Q3 after spiking due to the Russia-Ukraine disruptions—Indonesia now supplies over 50% of global Class 1 nickel, but we've de-risked with Australian and Canadian sources. Cobalt remains stable at $28,000 per metric ton, though ethical sourcing pressures from the DRC, which dominates 70% of supply, continue to weigh on margins.

Graphite anode material costs have been a positive development: synthetic graphite dropped 15% year-over-year to $8,500 per metric ton, but natural flake from China faces U.S. tariffs under Section 301, pushing us toward diversification. Steel and aluminum, more traditional auto inputs, saw 5-7% inflation due to energy costs in Europe, but our just-in-time inventory model kept working capital days at 45—well below the industry average of 60.

To manage this volatility, we've layered in a robust hedging program. As of quarter-end, 65% of our 2025 lithium needs are hedged at $14,200 per metric ton via swaps and collars with counterparties like Glencore and Trafigura. Nickel hedges cover 50% at $17,500 per metric ton, shielding us from LME spikes. This approach saved us $180 million in Q3 alone, or about $2.5 per kWh in pack-level savings.

Diversification is our north star. We've reduced single-country exposure: China now accounts for just 25% of our cell procurement, down from 45% in 2022, thanks to ramp-ups at our Nevada Gigafactory with Panasonic and our new South Carolina joint venture with LG Energy Solution. For cathodes, we're 60% NMC 811 from established suppliers like Umicore and BASF, but shifting 40% to LFP chemistries via CATL and BYD partnerships—LFP now powers 35% of our Atlas SUV lineup, cutting nickel and cobalt reliance by 70% and improving cold-weather range efficiency.

Key technical initiatives include upstream vertical integration: In Q2, we closed a $1.2 billion investment in a 50/50 JV with Piedmont Lithium for a North Carolina spodumene concentrator, securing 30,000 tonnes per annum of LCE starting 2026 at a fixed $800 per tonne conversion cost—30% below spot. This leverages IRA Section 45X credits, worth up to $40 per kWh in production tax incentives.

Recycling closed-loop systems through our Redwood Materials partnership hit 95% recovery rates on black mass processing last quarter, recycling 15,000 tonnes of end-of-life packs. This yields cathode precursors at 60% lower cost than virgin material, with scalability to 100,000 tonnes by 2027. We're targeting 20% recycled content in 2026 packs, aligning with EU Battery Regulation mandates.

We're also piloting alternative materials R&D, including sodium-ion cells with Faradion for entry-level models, which eliminate lithium entirely and use abundant sodium at $2,000 per tonne. Early tests show 150 Wh/kg density at $50 per kWh potential, de-risking against lithium's long-term supply crunch—global LCE production must triple to 2.5 million tonnes per annum by 2030 per IEA forecasts to meet 40% EV penetration.

Regionally, North America's resurgence is a game-changer. The Inflation Reduction Act has unlocked $3.5 billion in funding for our U.S. supply chain, with 80% of our 2025 battery metal needs now IRA-compliant—lithium from Albemarle's Kings Mountain restart, nickel from Talon Metals' Minnesota sulfide project. In Europe, where we've localized 40% of Bolt hatchback production in Germany, we're navigating CBAM carbon border taxes by sourcing low-carbon aluminum from Hydro's Norwegian smelters, shaving 10% off sheet costs.

Asia remains vital but managed: Long-term offtakes with Ganfeng for 50,000 tonnes per annum LCE through 2028 at escalating fixed prices starting at $13,000 per metric ton, and nickel intermediates from Tsingshan's Morowali Industrial Park in Indonesia, vetted for ESG compliance.

These efforts directly accreted to the bottom line: Raw material cost headwinds flipped to a $250 million tailwind in Q3, boosting adjusted EBITDA by 15% to $1.2 billion. Per-vehicle material costs for our flagship Zephyr sedan dropped to $12,500 from $15,200 year-over-year, enabling us to hold ASPs steady at $48,000 despite competitive pricing pressures from Tesla's Model Y and BYD's Seagull.

Looking ahead, we expect battery costs to decline another 12-15% in 2025, driven by scale—our cell production hit 25 GWh annualized in Q3—and falling precursor prices. Risks include potential lithium rebound if Chinese stimulus accelerates EV demand, or tariff escalations under a new U.S. administration. Mitigants: Expanding hedges to 75% coverage and advancing solid-state R&D with QuantumScape for 400 Wh/kg packs by 2028, targeting $50 per kWh.

Continuing with profitability metrics, let's drill down into gross margin per vehicle. This metric captures automotive gross profit—revenue less cost of goods sold, excluding regulatory credits—divided by total vehicle deliveries. It strips out variability from services, energy, or other segments, giving a pure read on our manufacturing and pricing efficiency at the unit level.

In Q3, we delivered 185,000 vehicles, up 28% year-over-year and 12% quarter-over-quarter, driven by the ramp of our NV1 mid-size SUV and NV2 crossover. Our average gross margin per vehicle reached $14,200, a record high and up 15% from Q2 and 112% improvement from Q3 2023. This translates to an overall automotive gross margin of 19.8%, expanding 420 basis points sequentially and 1,040 basis points year-over-year—putting us in line with Tesla's industry-leading 19-20% range, while peers like Rivian hover around negative territory and legacy players like Ford report EV-specific margins below 5%.

Revenue mix and ASP dynamics drove this: Our Q3 average selling price came in at $58,400, up quarter-over-quarter, reflecting a richer product mix: 62% NV1 SUVs at around $62,000 ASP, 32% NV2 crossovers at $48,000, and 6% premium NV0 sedans pushing $75,000-plus. We strategically held pricing firm in North America despite softening demand, aided by strong interest around our upcoming NV3 compact launch in early 2025. In contrast, Europe saw some ASP pressure from leasing discounts to counter BYD's aggressive pricing on the Atto 3, but our NV1's superior 520-mile EPA range and NACS compatibility kept take rates high.

On the cost side, COGS per vehicle fell to $44,200, down 8% quarter-over-quarter from scale efficiencies. Battery costs, our largest line item at 38% of COGS, improved to $112 per kWh at the pack level—a 22% year-over-year drop—thanks to our in-house 46-series cylindrical cells ramping at Gigafactory Nevada. We're now at 85% localization on LFP and NMC chemistries, reducing reliance on CATL and LG imports that plagued us in 2023 amid U.S. IRA tariff hikes to 25% on Chinese packs.

Powertrain and electronics were down 12% to $8,900 per unit via 800V architecture optimizations in the NV2, enabling faster charging and lower silicon carbide inverter costs. Our steer-by-wire and 48V mild-hybrid tech in the NV1 shaved another $450 per unit.

Labor and overhead benefited from fixed-cost leverage from Shanghai Gigafactory Phase 2 hitting 5,000 per week output, dropping per-unit factory costs by 18% to $4,200. U.S. lines at 95% OEE post our $250 million automation retrofit.

Regionally: North America, 75% of deliveries, saw $16,800 per vehicle margin, up 20% quarter-over-quarter, fueled by IRA-compliant U.S. content exceeding 60%—unlocking $7,500 tax credits per NV1. California demand surged 55% on ZEV mandates. Europe, 18%, at $11,200, pressured by tariffs but offset by our Berlin plant's local sourcing of 40% modules. Our OTA-upgradable Full Autonomy Package at $12,000 added $2,500 per unit margin kicker. China/APAC, 7%, at $9,500, challenged by the price war but with cost parity via joint-venture efficiencies.

These gains stem from our VertiScale initiative: vertical integration targeting 75% self-supply by 2026. We've clawed back 600 basis points from outsourcing via in-house seat frames, chassis castings—Giga Press yielding 40% material savings—and thermal management. Q4 guidance calls for $15,000 to $15,500 per vehicle on 210,000 to 220,000 deliveries, assuming stable ASP and COGS at $43,000 per unit. Tailwinds: 4680 cell qualification complete, cutting energy density costs another 15%; supply chain de-risking post Red Sea disruptions; and FSD-like software attach rates to 45%.

Risks include commodity volatility—lithium spot at $12,000 per tonne could add $300 per unit if unhedged—intensifying China competition, and potential U.S. election impacts on IRA subsidies. But our $3.2 billion cash position gives us runway to invest in next-gen silicon anode batteries for 20% plus margins by 2026.

Now, on delivery volume guidance by model, which reflects our sharpened focus on execution amid a dynamic EV landscape. Q3 deliveries beat prior guidance by 5,000 units, thanks to supply chain efficiencies that boosted Shanghai Gigafactory output by 15% sequentially.

Looking ahead, we're guiding for Q4 total deliveries of 210,000 to 220,000 units, implying 14-19% quarter-over-quarter growth and 35-40% year-over-year growth. This puts full-year 2024 deliveries at 780,000 to 790,000 units, a robust 45% year-over-year increase from 2023's 540,000 units. Breaking it down by model:

Spark Compact Hatchback, our entry-level hero priced at $28,000 to $32,000 post-IRA incentives: Q3 saw 42,000 deliveries, up 20% year-over-year on fleet sales to partners like Uber and Hertz. Q4 guidance: 48,000 to 50,000 units, 14% quarter-over-quarter growth. FY25 outlook: 190,000 to 200,000 units annually, buoyed by a 10% cost reduction from next-gen LFP packs sourced 80% from CATL, dropping to under $55 per kWh. U.S. volumes grow 25% on 40% lease penetration; Europe softens slightly due to subsidy phase-outs but offset by UK ZEV mandates.

Bolt Mid-Size Sedan, with 4680 cell integration for 350-plus miles EPA at $38,000 ASP: Q3 35,000 units. Q4: 42,000 to 45,000, 20-29% growth. FY25: 160,000 to 170,000, fueled by NovaMind ADAS suite at Level 3 beta, unlocking $2,500 upsell. China 60% of volumes, up 50% year-over-year; U.S. 30% growth on credits.

Surge Mid-Size SUV/Crossover, our volume kingpin with 400-mile range at $45,000 to $52,000 ASP: Q3 78,000, up 55% year-over-year. Q4: 90,000 to 95,000. FY24 to 320,000-plus; FY25 380,000 to 400,000, supported by Texas Gigafactory Line 3 at 5,000 per week. SUVs now 55% mix; U.S. family hauler demand amid gas price hikes; Europe 25,000 Q4 units; China rebounds with Blade battery refresh.

Thunder Full-Size Pickup, high-margin at $65,000 to $85,000 ASP with 500-mile range: Q3 debut 30,000 units. Q4: 28,000 to 30,000. FY25: 120,000 to 140,000, targeting F-150 Lightning share. 48V accessories for 15% gains; U.S.-centric at 85% volumes.

This model mix shifts premium-ward: FY25 ASP $48,000 to $50,000, up 5% year-over-year, with Thunder and Surge at 35% margins vs. Spark's 22%. Capacity expands 40% to 1.2 million via Berlin Phase 2 and U.S. expansions. Risks: China normalization; upside: $1.2 billion regulatory credits, backlog up 15%. U.S. 45% Q4 mix, China 30%, Europe 20%, Rest 5%. We're positioned for 25% plus CAGR.

Shifting to factory expansions and operational efficiency improvements, foundational to scaling while preserving margins. We're on track with $4.2 billion CapEx for FY24, 60% to expansions. Nevada Gigafactory Phase 2 adds 40 GWh by Q4 2025, total 100 GWh for 4680 cells, co-locating to slash logistics 15-20%.

Europe: $1.1 billion Berlin-Brandenburg for 250,000 units by 2026, LFP focus for EU compliance. Asia: $800 million Shanghai for 400,000 units, 85% local sourcing. Group capacity from 850,000 to 1.8 million by 2026, CapEx intensity 8% of revenue.

Efficiency: Plants at 92% utilization, targeting 95%. Smart Factory 2.0 with 5,000 AI vision systems and cobots. Giga Press XL reduces part count 400 to 70, takt time 28% to under 10 hours, costs $1,200 less per unit. Dry electrode coating: energy 40% less, yield 98%, cost $65 per kWh.

U.S.: IRA localization cuts working capital 18 days, $450 million PTC Q3. Europe: 30% renewables. China: inventory 12x turns. Future-proofing for L4 with 800V, zonal ECUs reducing wiring 50%. Expect 22% margins FY25, ROIC 25% on CapEx.

Before moving on, a note on the impact of raw material costs and supply chain disruptions shaping our P&L. These headwinds contributed to COGS pressures, but we've limited damage. Battery precursors drove inflation: lithium at $13,500 per ton, up from 2021 but down from peaks; nickel at $16,500 after spikes; aluminum surcharges 15%. Raw materials 62% of EV COGS, compressing per-vehicle profit $1,200.

Disruptions: Red Sea added $1,500 per FEU, delaying 15,000 units, $45 million writedowns; Panama droughts inflated logistics 22%. North America shielded by IRA Ohio gigafactory; Europe nickel delays; China flat on LFP.

Mitigations: 75% 2025-2026 lithium offtakes at $12,000 per ton; 35% LFP shift to $85 per kWh; hub-and-spoke reduces lead times 40%; sodium-ion pilots; Redwood recycling 5 GWh Q2, 95% yield; 60% hedging. Expect cooling to 4-6% inflation H2, margins to 21%.

Finally, an update on supply chain constraints and mitigation strategies. Q3 disruptions shaved 18% off targets, 45,000 vehicle shortfall, $320 million revenue hit. Battery cells up 12% availability, but semis 28-32 weeks; lithium $45,000 per ton peak. North America port congestion; Europe Red Sea 22% freight hike; Asia cathode delays.

Mitigations clawed back 65%: Supplier diversification—semis from GlobalFoundries/Renesas at 16-week leads; batteries 40% LG U.S., 25% CATL Hungary, Northvolt 20 GWh 2025. Vertical: Nevada Phase 2 60 GWh; Wolfspeed SiC JV. Inventory three months chips; AI platform 92% accuracy. Zonal architectures cut chips 30%; CTP zero cobalt 40% packs; reshoring fund.

Tesla/Ford peers struggle more; our margin held. Normalization Q1 2025. $5 billion liquidity for opportunities.

Next, I'll hand the call over to Dr. Liam Chen for an update on our manufacturing operations.

Dr. Liam Chen:
Thank you, Marcus. Our manufacturing facilities are operating at peak efficiency to meet the growing demand for our vehicles. We have successfully implemented several lean manufacturing principles, resulting in improved throughput and reduced lead times, with OEE now at 95% across key lines. Our expansions in Nevada, Berlin, and Shanghai are ramping ahead of schedule, leveraging Giga Press and dry electrode tech to drive down costs while scaling to 1.8 million units by 2026. We are confident in our ability to scale production further as needed, supporting our delivery guidance and margin goals.

Following me, Sophia Grant will provide insights into our technological advancements.

Sophia Grant:
Thank you. We continue to invest heavily in research and development to maintain our technological edge. Our advancements in battery technology—like 4680 cells, LFP shifts, and solid-state pilots with QuantumScape—and autonomous driving systems, including NovaMind ADAS at Level 3 with OTA upgrades, are positioning us as a leader in the EV industry. We're embedding 800V architectures and zonal ECUs for software-defined vehicles, enhancing efficiency and enabling high-margin features.

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. To withdraw, star then two.

Analyst 1:
Hi, thanks for taking my question. On raw material hedging and the JV with Piedmont Lithium, can you elaborate on how that's impacting 2025 margins, especially with potential lithium rebounds?

Elena Vasquez:
Great question. Our hedging at $14,200 per ton for 65% of 2025 needs, combined with the Piedmont JV securing LCE at $800 per tonne conversion—30% below spot—directly supports our 12-15% battery cost decline guidance. With IRA credits up to $40 per kWh, this should add 200-300 basis points to margins, insulating us even if lithium rebounds on Chinese demand.

Analyst 2:
Thanks. Regarding gross margin per vehicle regional variances, how sustainable is the North America premium with IRA credits amid election risks?

Marcus Hale:
North America's $16,800 per vehicle is sustainable with 60% plus U.S. content unlocking $7,500 credits, but we're preparing for scenarios. Our localization roadmap to 75% self-supply by 2026 reduces reliance, and software like Full Autonomy Package adds durable $2,500 uplift. Election risks are in our guidance conservatism.

Analyst 3:
On factory expansions, what's the CapEx phasing for Berlin and Nevada, and expected OEE there?

Dr. Liam Chen:
Berlin's $1.1 billion is phased 40% this year for pilot lines at 25% utilization now, full 250,000 units by 2026 with EU-compliant LFP. Nevada Phase 2 $ spend is front-loaded, targeting 100 GWh total with 95% OEE via AI cobots and Giga Press. Overall CapEx 8% of revenue keeps us efficient.

Analyst 4:
For delivery guidance, any color on Thunder pickup supply constraints and FY25 truck market share goals?

Sophia Grant:
Thunder's flat-to-up Q4 reflects casting constraints like Cybertruck, but 48V and structural packs position us well. FY25 120k-140k targets 10% U.S. EV truck share, gaining on F-150 Lightning via fleet wins and 500-mile range.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for your questions. We have time for two more.

Analyst 5:
Supply chain-wise, how are Red Sea and Panama issues affecting Q4, and what's the inventory buffer?

Elena Vasquez:
Red Sea reroutes added costs but our hub-and-spoke and three-month stockpiles mitigated, with AI forecasting preempting 70%. Q4 impacts minimal as we've diversified to LG U.S. and Northvolt, restoring 92% production attainment.

Analyst 6:
Finally, on impact of disruptions, how does LFP shift and recycling offset cobalt/nickel volatility long-term?

Marcus Hale:
LFP at 35% of mix cuts nickel/cobalt 70%, stabilizing at $85/kWh, while Redwood's 95% recovery on 15k tonnes recycled yields 60% cheaper precursors. Sodium-ion pilots add no-lithium optionality, targeting 20% margins as we scale recycled content to 20% by 2026.

Operator:
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Elena Vasquez for closing remarks.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are excited about the opportunities ahead and remain committed to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We look forward to sharing our progress with you next quarter.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the NovaVolt Motors Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
